identity.title: Perception Encoder: The best visual embeddings are not at the output of the network

problem.claim: Develop general-purpose vision encoders for image and video understanding across diverse downstream tasks.

contributions.claim: Introduces Perception Encoder, using contrastive vision-language pretraining plus language and spatial alignment to expose useful intermediate representations.
Reports that contrastive vision-language training alone can produce strong general embeddings across the described downstream tasks, with embeddings located in intermediate layers.
Releases models, code, and a dataset of synthetically and human-annotated videos.

stated_novelty.claim: The work distinguishes itself by extracting task-useful visual embeddings from intermediate network layers and aligning them for multimodal language modeling and dense prediction.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report state-of-the-art results across zero-shot image/video classification and retrieval, document/image/video question answering, detection, tracking, and depth estimation.

The authors report that scaling a tuned image-pretraining recipe and refining it with a robust video data engine makes contrastive vision-language training alone yield strong general embeddings for the listed tasks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Vision encoders traditionally use different pretraining objectives, each excelling at different downstream tasks.
The authors report that scaled, tuned contrastive vision-language training can instead produce strong general embeddings, but these embeddings reside in intermediate layers.
PE introduces language alignment for multimodal language modeling and spatial alignment for dense prediction to draw out those representations.
The authors report state-of-the-art performance across classification, retrieval, question answering, and spatial tasks, and release models, code, and video data.

source_observation.claim: The abstract identifies a mismatch between where useful embeddings reside and the network output, then pairs separate alignment methods with multimodal language modeling and dense prediction.

lessons.interpretation: A representation can be broadly useful even when it is not exposed at the default output; downstream alignment can be framed around the representation location and task structure.
lessons.application: When presenting a general encoder, explicitly inspect or motivate intermediate representations and map each extraction or alignment mechanism to the downstream task type.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the target task or architecture requires only the final representation, or when intermediate-layer utility has not been measured.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify benchmark names, numerical results, dataset sizes, or evaluation conditions behind the state-of-the-art claims.
It does not quantify how much the alignment methods contribute relative to the base encoder or alternative layer choices.
